title: Ten Days Before Kickoff, India Finally Has a World Cup Broadcaster. Here Is What It Means for NRI Fans.
excerpt: Zee Entertainment's last-minute $60 million deal secures FIFA rights through 2034. For diaspora viewers in the US, UK, and Canada, Zee5 streaming is the answer.
body:
The 2026 FIFA World Cup kicks off on June 11 in Mexico City. Until four days ago, 1.4 billion Indians — and millions more in the diaspora — did not know where they would watch it.

That changed on June 1, when FIFA announced an eight-year broadcast partnership with Zee Entertainment Enterprises. The deal covers 39 FIFA events from 2026 through 2034, including the 2026 and 2030 World Cups, the 2027 Women's World Cup, and a slate of youth and futsal tournaments. Financial terms were not officially disclosed, but Reuters reported that FIFA initially sought roughly $100 million for the India package before settling at approximately $60 million.

## The Channels

Zee is launching a brand-new sports network for the occasion: Unite8 Sports. Four linear channels — Unite8 Sports 1 and Unite8 Sports 1 HD in Hindi, Unite8 Sports 2 and Unite8 Sports 2 HD in English — will carry the live matches on television. For digital viewers, Zee5 is the primary streaming platform.

This is a significant departure from the 2022 World Cup cycle, when Viacom18 handled Indian coverage through Sports18 and JioCinema. Fans who assumed the same broadcasters would carry the 2026 edition were caught off guard by the prolonged uncertainty.

## Why It Took So Long

Negotiations between FIFA and the Indian market had been stalled for months. JioStar, the Reliance-Disney joint venture that inherited Viacom18's sports portfolio, was among the interested parties but reportedly submitted an offer of around $20 million — well below FIFA's expectations. Sony, which held the rights for the 2014 and 2018 editions, held discussions but never made a formal bid.

India had become one of the last major unsold markets for the tournament. The standoff reflected a broader tension: FIFA's valuation of the Indian football audience versus the commercial reality of a market where cricket still commands the overwhelming majority of sports advertising spend. Zee's willingness to pay $60 million — even at a discount from the original ask — signals a strategic bet on football's growing Indian fanbase.

## What This Means for NRI Viewers

For Indian diaspora communities in North America, the UK, and the Gulf, the Zee5 platform is the most accessible option. The streaming service is available globally, and the tournament's North American time zone — the World Cup is co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico — means many matches will air at convenient hours for US-based viewers.

The deal also comes with documentary programming tied to FIFA competitions, which Zee has said will be tailored for Indian audiences. Whether that extends to Hindi and regional-language commentary for all 104 matches remains to be seen.

## The Indian Connection on the Pitch

While India's men's team is not at the tournament, the diaspora will have its own rooting interests. Four players of Indian heritage — Sarpreet Singh (New Zealand), Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid (Qatar), Nishan Velupillay (Australia), and Samuel Moutoussamy (DR Congo) — have been named in their respective national squads.

Jamshid's story is particularly resonant. The 19-year-old winger was born in Doha to Malayali parents from Kannur, Kerala. He plays for Al-Duhail in the Qatari Stars League and has already been hailed by MP Shashi Tharoor as the first Keralite to reach football's grandest stage.

## Zee's Bigger Play

For Zee Entertainment, this is more than a one-tournament acquisition. The company exited sports broadcasting roughly eight years ago when it sold its sports assets to Sony. The Unite8 Sports launch marks a full re-entry, with plans to carry not just football but also kabaddi, cricket, badminton, wrestling, boxing, and combat sports.

Zee shares rose approximately 7 percent following the announcement. The market appears to have endorsed the strategy — or at least acknowledged that owning the World Cup, even at the last minute, is a powerful brand play.

The first ball is kicked in Mexico City in eight days. Indian fans, at home and abroad, finally know where to find it.

*Sources: FIFA official announcement; Reuters; Inc42; Athlon Sports; Sporting News India*
